the Northampton election will be a success, "Lady Fanny Perpoint
has made some discourse again" by eloping from the opera under

Mary Wortley's. She reports a death, a lying in, and a bad case
of smallpox.

docs.dcterms_abstract:
She congratulates "my brother and your ladyship" on the success at
Northampton and is anxiously awaiting news of the elections at
Tamworth and Evesham. The letter is all about various people: a
birth to Lady Guilford: a lady's refusal: quarrel: a death:
birthday greetings to Lord Northampton.

ox_transcription: Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Sinéad Duffy , edited by Sarah Ward. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Anne Rushout to Elizabeth Compton 30 April 1734 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries , MS Eng. Letters e. 2, fols 7–8 To the Right Honourable the Countess of Northampton at Castle Ashby Northampton Ashby Bagg London April 30th 1734 Dear Madam I am very glad to have the oppe rtunity to Congratulate my Br other and your Ladyship on your good success at Northampton I am extream glad the trouble is over as we wished, I hope from Tamworth to hear the sam e good news ; at this time I am a little anxious for the success at Evesham \some of this days/ Dayly papers say Sir John has lost it, but I had intelegence from himself yesterday with better account & I believe they can have none of later date; to morrow s post I shall wait with impatience, my Brother Gore seems mighty well, and also please d to have surmounted his trouble & come to London again; where I believe we shall have more company when this week is over, the small pox continues still very much Miss Windam had a terrible sort & died Sunday Morn Lady Guildford has it now it appear’ d the day after being delivered (of a Dau ghter) . Tis said she is as well as can be Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Sinéad Duffy , edited by Sarah Ward. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 expected; Lady Fanny Pierpoints escape from Mrs St George at the Opera was a very shor t wonder, the whole nine days was over upon her refusal of Mr Spencer Last Y ear, her excuse was she was not well & had need to go out, Miss Wortle y went with her & she took Hartshorn drops and got into a Chair; Lady Mary has had a tight quarrel with Mrs St George about it ; the Widow Lady Monson is dead her will not yet opened Lord Paulet was expected in town last night or today, I must take this opper tunity to beg your Ladyship to present my humble service to Lord Northampton and wish him abundance of joy on his birthday and heartily wish he may live to see the return of a great Many m ore and that your Ladyship & all your family may L ong be partakers with him of joy on that day; I wont yet quite fix my journy to Sc arborough for had rather not go, but am so much advised to it that I c ant say positively I will not. I believe you find it very pleasant in the C ountry and I hope the Y oung Ladys are all well I beg my service for them and Lady Betty and am Dear Madam Your Most affectionate1 humble servant A Rushout My Little G irl begs her duty to your lordship my Ladyship & service to all Ladys. 1 The word ‘affectionate ’ is covered partially by wax .

rest of the letter she recommends a man who has had charge of Mr.
Ashby's 10 year old son, and has served Mrs. Pitt who recommends
him.

docs.dcterms_abstract:
She refers to a fire in Albemarle Street. London is not yet empty,
but Lady Rushout and Lady Northampton are soon leaving. The weather
has. been too cold and wet to go to Kensington Gardens. The court
is soon coming from Richmond to Kensington where the Queen will be
while the King goes abroad. She tells of two marriages among the
aristocracy.

ox_transcription: Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Charlotte Leung Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 M. Compton to Elizabeth Compton 1st June 1734 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries, MS Eng. letters e. 2. fols 17 -18. Dover Street June 1st 1734 It was very obligeing in Dear Lady Northampton to remember the 30th, I return you a great many thanks, for your kind wishes to me upon that day and also for the favour of your Letter; it is very much to be wished, that it was discovered how the fire happened in Albermarle Street, there is a great many reports about it, but now it is generally agreed, it was done by a Servant, that had lived with Mr Cantillion, had left him about three Weeks, and was let into the House, by some other of the Servants for he came back to where he Lodged just at the time of the Fire, they say he brought with him a great deal of Money, and a Portmanteau, he came for the rest of his things, and said he had only waited for a fair Wind, and went Post directly, it was re - ported he was taken at Dover, but I fear t hat is not true, for have not heard it confirmed; I dont think the town is very empty, but believe next Week, I shall find it more so, for Lady Anne Rushout, goes Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Charlotte Leung Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 Monday, and Lady Northampton, some day that Week to Harrow, I never think the town empty, as long as any of my Friends are in it, and I think one meets them the oftener, when it is not altogether so full, if it is not better Weather in the Country, then we have here, I am sure it can be no temptation, for any body to go down for I never saw the begining of a Summer so unplea - -sant, as this, we have had no Weather at all. for Walking, so Cold and so Wett, there has been no going to Kensington Gardens, and the Court comes so soon that there will be very little opportunity of doing Now they talk very much of the Kings going abroad and if so Her Majesty, always stays at Kensington at that time; they say they are very impatient to come that they may see a little Company again, for they are very sick of their Retirement, for so long at Richmond I hea r Sr William Wyndham was Marryed last Thursday to Lady Blandford; Lady Caroline Manners Wedding will not be yet some time, it is to be at Stapleford in Leicestershire, and you know the Dss Rutland is not very steady in her Resolutions, and has not absolutely fixed her time for going out of Town; the Duke of Portland is very soon to be Marryed, I think, these are all the Weddings I have heard on; I beg my Humble Service to my Brother, Lord Compton, and all the Ladys Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Charlotte Leung Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 3 and I am Dear Madam Your Ladysps Obedient Humble Servant Lady Pen desires M Compton her Service to your Ladysp and all the familey at Ashby.

ox_transcription: Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Charlotte Leung , edited by Sarah Ward. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Penelope Compton to Elizabeth Compton 6 July 1734 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries, MS Eng. letters e. 2, fols 13 –14 Dover Street July 6th 1734 I am always glad of any opportunity of hearing that Dear Lady Northampton and all Friends at Ashby are well and Yesterday had that satisfaction by the Person who brought the Venison you were so good to send us for which we both are very much obliged and return my Brother and you many thanks for it, an d must also now congratulate your Lady ship upon this day wishing you much joy of Lord Comptons Birth -day and that he may see a great many of them, I was sorry to hear of your accidents but hope you did not receive much hurt, tho it is a little discouragei ng and so may take off the pleasure of Rideing for some time, and beleive you have had but indifferent weather for most people that are in the Country complain of it, and here we have had but few warm days tho that can be mighty well dispensed with in Lond on for it makes it less dusty then usual at this time of Year, tho last thursday met with a good deal going to Chiswick when my Lord Wilmington did us the favour to invite us to dine with him, his L ordship is mighty well and talks of going into Sussex again some time the end of the Summer; the Princess of Orange had a very bad Passage back for the Wind was preety high and not very fair neither so they were obliged to land at the very first place they cou’d get a shore so that she was very indifferently acc omadated for was forced to come in a stage coach and got to Kensington at three a clock in the morning, which surprised them all much, I hear she looks thin but have not seen her yet for except Sundays and Thursdays there is not a creature and you know then the drawing Rooms are not very agreable so chose to deffer it and intend going to morrow, Lady Mary Tryant is gone into Northamptonshire she was in town for 2 or 3 days in her way thither, Mrs Shirley lyes Inn of a Daughter and is very well, the great wedding in our Neighbourhood is not yet over tho there has been several days named for it, but they say it won’t be till the week after next I beg your Lady ship will do me Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Charlotte Leung , edited by Sarah Ward. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 the favour to present my humble service to Lord Northampton and all the Ladys and Lady Margaret desires the same to [XXX ] and beleive me [Rest of letter is damaged. ]

docs.dcterms_abstract:
London is very hot and empty, so she and Lady Margaret have taken
a house at Bracknell (10 guineas till Christmas) at the end of the
village in the forest affording walks which are very agreeable
after being shut out of Kensington gardens all this year: whereas
the Park is dusty and not safe, for two ladies were robbed in the
Queen's new walk. She writes of comings and goings of various
aristocrats and their families; of a dangerous childbirth; of a
wedding with entertainment of music on the water.

Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Penelope Compton to Elizabeth Compton 27 July 1734 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries, MS Eng. Letters e. 2, fols 15–16 Dover Street July 27th 1734 Whilst Dear Lady Northampton was from Ashby it was of no purpose to write but as this is about the time that you proposed to return wou’ d not defer ackn owledg eing the favour of your oblig eing Letter and beg you to accept of my thanks for it being always extream ly glad to hear from y our Ladyship and hope that you have had a good journey and that this will find you all very well after it, I dare say Lady Jane had great pleasure in being one of the company and made it more agreable to all ; I fancy some days you found it very hot travelling , for we have thought it so here this last week which makes the town very disagre able besides its being vastly empty, so Lady Margaret an d I have taken a little house at Bracknel not far from Windsor which stands plea santly enough, and we give but a small matter for it, for there is very good conveniency’s and a Kitchin G arden and we have it till Xtmas for 10 Guinea ’s, it is at the end of a little Village in the Fo rest so that there is very good walking about it, which I fancy we shall think very agre able hav eing been all this year shut out of Kensing ton Gardens which is a L oss to those that stay in London for one can ’t have much sweet A ir in the park it is dusty and besides Ladys will be afraid there, for two Mr Trevors wer e robbed last week in the Queen s new walk about 8 a clock, but the M an was taken so it is to be hoped that will det er others from attempting it; poor Lady Frederick has had a very bad Lyeing - Inn and is in a good deal of danger for continues sti ll mighty with a fever, it is well Mrs Duncomb was not catched the C ountry for think she ventured pree ty fair for it for c ame to town but of the Fryday and was brought to Bed the Mu nday follow ing, but they say she is very well. Sir F rancis Shipworth was married last Tuesday, the Duke and Dutchess of Portland are still at my Lord Oxfords , but soon to go to Bolstred, there was a Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Sinéad Duffy , edited by Sarah Ward. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 great deal of finery at that wedding, and t’o ther night they had an entertainment and Musick upon the W ater; I hear Lord Hallifax and his famly are gone down to Horton and Mr & Mrs Montague with them , which I doubt is no good sign, for it looks as if they intended to pursue their design of being still more troub lesom to you at Northampton, which I am very sorry for, I fancy you won’t be very good neighbours all this year; I had a letter from Lisbon about a week a goe and our F riends there were all very well, as was Lord Compton last Tuesday when we sent to him; I beg my hum ble service to my Brother and the Lady’ s, whe never your Ladyship is so good to favour me with a L etter please to direct as usual in Dover Street and they will be conveyed to us for we prop ose going next week, but hope to have the plea sure of hearing from you sometimes which will always be esteemed a great satisfaction by Dear Lady Northampton Your Affectionate sister and Obedient servant Pen: Compton Lady Margaret presents her humble service to my Lord and your Ladyship

Pessers to Elizabeth Compton 21 September 1734 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries, MS Eng. letters e. 2, fol. 67 [Addressed] To the Right Honourable the Contess of Northampton Madame jespere que votre Grandeur ne ce rapas faschée -daprendre que je suis come resusitée puis quapres a voir este a lextrémité par les dou leurs que je sentois an stomac é an la tai tes car mon rumatisme ma voit remonte mais d epuis lundy dernier jes este tou les jours a meribon la promenade ma fait un bien in magienable e qui pris une chambre pour un mois dons jes pere me -redone re \la/ sante in su madame je vous prie de vous sou ve nir que la St Michel ce ra bien tos eque votre Grandeu r a oublie la pauvre pesen c etteste mais apresent que je suis an convalais sanse je pourais manger quel que chosse qui na pa este Croque jes pere que toute votre jlustre familie et [[XXX]] par faitte sentés je suis Madame de votre Grandeur Latre humble etré Son mise obeysante Servant e Ma Pessers alon dre se 21e Septembre 1734

and can scarcely eat: Her Ladyship's kind present of butter has
been very opportune. She is poor and alone. Her lottery tickets
have all been blanks.

docs.dcterms_abstract:
The letter consists of items of personal and topical news e.g.
the Countess Dowager of Northampton has received a New Year's gift
from Her Majesty, who was concerned because of her long confinement
by gout, and the Countess is fussed how to return such an honour;
and Lady Longueville's journey to town has been delayed by flooded
roads and the danger of smallpox obliging her to avoid Northampton
and make a long circuit.

ox_transcription: Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Charlotte Leung , edited by Sarah Ward . Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Elizabeth Compton to unnamed recipient 2 January 173 5 SOURCE: Bodleian Librarie s, MS Eng. letters e. 2, fols 1 –2 London Jan uary the 2nd-1734/35 Dear Madam I am very glad to think I shall so soon have the pleasure of seeing your Ladyship in Town, but cannot forbear taking an opportunity of wishing y ou a good journey, & giving thanks for the favour of your Letter & acknowledging my obligations for the many good wishes so kindly sent in it. I was sorry to hear my Brother & Lady Anne had both been out of order but hope that they are both very well again. to be laid by the Heels had an odd sound for a Peer of the Realm; to be tied by the Legg or Toe, might have entituled him to a Sovera ign Remedy & yet perhaps the Earl might have gone without, tho’ the Countess Dowager of Northampton was yesterday morning much surpriz ed at a message & a new - years -Gift from her Majesty, concerned at her being so long confin ’d by the Gout, sent her such a Wheeling Chair as she had so often found of great service to her , she hoped she would do the same. my Lady was in great fuss last night to know which way she was to return so great an honour, not being able to go out, whether by Letter to th e Lady of the Bedchamber? or how? at last it was determined that Lady Jane as living with her was the properest person to make her compliments. so this morning she was t o go to St James’s. your Ladyship was pleased to joke upon us Londoners for being able to send news never any correspondant you had knew less than I, nor I believe less authentick. for remember I sent word of a report said to be made by Dr Douglass which is now quite contradicted, & that t he Princess goes on purely well: therefore the Birth of the Son & He ir, & little maid that you sent me word off was news to me & true, which is more than one durst hardly vouch for any that one hears here. my Brother George is just come to Town very well, & desires his most humble service to my Brother & your Ladyship. poo r Tom Warren died on Tuesday last a mortification in his other Leg. I almost every day fear to hear that poor Lady Frederick does of one in her Bowells. she is very ill but full of spiritts, tho’ in continual pain. Elizabeth Compton correspondence Transcription by Charlotte Leung , edited by Sarah Ward . Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 Lady Longueville is expected in Town to night, but obliged to make four days what she used to come in three, not so much from the badness of the Roads, which are terrible by the floods, but that she is forced to break her Stages, upon the account of Mastr Yelverton’s not having had the Small -Pox it being so much at Northampton & Newport -Pagnell, she darest not stop at either. I beg my most humble service to my Lords & Ladys & to be esteemed Dear Madam Your most affectionat Sister & Servant E: Compton
